content: Citronella oil is an essential oil derived from the leaves and stems of various species of the Cymbopogon plant. It is widely utilized as a source of perfumery chemicals, including citronellal, citronellol, and geraniol. These compounds are extensively used in the production of soaps, perfumes, cosmetics, and flavoring agents across the globe. Additionally, citronella oil is a well-known plant-based insect repellent and has been registered for this purpose in the United States since 1948. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) classifies citronella oil as a biopesticide with a non-toxic mode of action. Research has also demonstrated its potent antifungal properties and its effectiveness in calming barking dogs. Citronella oil is commercially categorized into two chemotypes: 1. Ceylon type: This type is extracted from Cymbopogon nardus Rendle and contains geraniol (18–20%), limonene (9–11%), methyl isoeugenol (7–11%), citronellol (6–8%), and citronellal (5–15%). 2. Java type: This type is obtained from Cymbopogon winterianus Jowitt and is composed of citronellal (32–45%), geraniol (11–13%), geranyl acetate (3–8%), and limonene (1–4%). The Java type, due to its higher concentrations of geraniol and citronellal, is considered a superior source for perfumery derivatives. The name Cymbopogon winterianus was given to honor Mr. Winter, a prominent oil distiller in Ceylon who first cultivated and distilled the Maha Pangeri variety of citronella in the region. Both types are believed to have originated from Mana Grass in Ceylon, which exists in two wild forms: Cymbopogon nardus var. linnae (typicus) and C. nardus var. confertiflorus. However, neither wild form is significantly used for oil distillation. It is important to note that citronella oil from Cymbopogon species should not be confused with other lemon-scented oils derived from Corymbia citriodora or Pelargonium citrosum. Currently, global production of citronella oil is approximately 7,000 tonnes annually. Major producers include Taiwan, Guatemala, Honduras, Indonesia, Brazil, China, Sri Lanka, India, Argentina, Ecuador, Madagascar, Mexico, and the West Indies. Citronella oil is widely recognized as a natural insect repellent. Its effectiveness in repelling mosquitoes, including Aedes aegypti, has been validated by research. However, most citronella-based repellents applied to the skin require reapplication every 30–60 minutes to maintain efficacy. While citronella oil is generally safe, it may cause skin irritation or dermatitis in some individuals. It is not recommended for use on the skin of young children under the age of three. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has stated that citronella oil has minimal to no toxicity when used as a topical insect repellent, with no significant adverse effects reported over a 60-year period. The EPA mandates proper precautionary labeling to ensure safe use. When used according to label instructions in the U.S., citronella oil is not expected to pose health risks to humans, including children and other sensitive populations. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies citronella oil as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS). In Canada, regulatory concerns regarding citronella oil as an insect repellent are primarily due to gaps in toxicological data rather than reported incidents. In Europe, Ceylon-type citronella oil is categorized as a Class 3 substance due to safety concerns related to methyl eugenol content.
